newsitem.title: GERMANY: German police troll for illicit Internet material.
newsitem.headline: German police troll for illicit Internet material.

text.p: Alarmed over the availability of pornography and extremist writings on the Internet, German investigators have set up teams of cybersleuths to surf the Net in search of illicit material.

The Munich state prosecutor's office, which has indicted the head of Compuserve's German unit in connection with child pornography on the Internet, has five officials who spend the day trolling for obscene pictures, Nazi diatribes and other material banned in Germany.
"We document what we find, copy it and print it out and turn it over to the investigators," said Karl-Heinz Moewes, chief criminal officer for the Internet operation.

Other states also have teams of cybersleuths, while officials in the federal government and local police also patrol cyberspace for pornography involving children and animals, Nazi writings and other materials that glorify violence, which are illegal in Germany.

The Munich office, one of the few full-time anti- internet-pornography staffs in Germany, last year uncovered postings that led to 110 cases, two-thirds involving material from outside Germany, Moewes said.
Prosecutors in other German states search the global computer network when cases arise, he said.
Moewes' team finds most illegal material not on the World Wide Web -- a popular portion of the Internet where it is easy to display pictures -- but in an older and more arcane area called Usenet.

Usenet contains forums, or newsgroups, dedicated to nearly any subject imaginable, from stamp collecting to UFOs. In these newsgroups, computer users correspond by typing messages and posting computer files that to novice users appear to be only long strings of numbers.
More experienced users post Usenet files that can be downloaded and reformatted into images, and it is these types of files that the five Munich officers sift through daily.
"We are a service bureau," Moewes said. "We find the material, but we have no way of removing this material."
Since the material can be made available on the Internet from a computer anywhere in the world, blocking access is very difficult, he said.

German authorities have targeted online companies like Compuserve and internet access providers like EUnet. These companies say they want to cooperate with authorities, but online providers should not be held responsible for all material posted on the Internet.

"If users break German law, we cooperate with the authorities," said Ingo Reese, a spokesman for AOL Deutschland, a venture of America Online Inc. and German media group Bertelsmann. "We will offer subscriber data that we can give out in accordance with the data protection laws."

A spokesman for T-Online, a unit of Deutsche Telekom AG and Germany's largest online service, said online companies should police the content they host, but controlling material from other users or even other countries is difficult.
